learn.intro: How could a few hundred Spanish soldiers bring down the Mexica (Aztec) Empire? And why did the Portuguese have such a different experience when Vasco da Gama entered the Indian Ocean? This topic compares two very different encounters.

sections.title: 1. The fall of the Mexica Empire

blocks.p: In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with roughly 500–600 Spanish soldiers. By 1521 the Mexica (Aztec) Empire, ruling millions from its capital Tenochtitlan, one of the largest cities in the world, had fallen. A small force defeating a huge empire needs several causes:

ul: ALLIANCES: many peoples resented Mexica rule. The Tlaxcalans, long-standing enemies of the Mexica, allied with Cortés and provided tens of thousands of warriors, arguably the biggest single factor.
DISEASE: smallpox devastated the Mexica, killing the emperor Cuitláhuac in 1520 at a critical moment.
TECHNOLOGY: steel weapons, some firearms and horses gave real but often overstated advantages.
POLITICS: Mexica caution and internal tensions gave Cortés time to build alliances.

blocks.p: Historians usually judge Indigenous alliances and disease the most significant. The popular idea that Spanish weapons alone won is a myth that erases the Indigenous allies who vastly outnumbered the Spanish.

evidence: Cortés landed in 1519 with about 500–600 soldiers.

blocks.p: In 1498 Vasco da Gama's fleet rounded Africa and reached Calicut on India's west coast, the first European ships to sail directly from Europe to India.

He did not arrive in an unconnected world. Calicut, ruled by the Zamorin, was part of the sophisticated Indian Ocean trading world. Da Gama's cheap trade goods did not impress, and established Arab merchants were rivals.

Because Portugal could not out-compete these merchants by trade alone, it turned to force: naval violence and fortified trading posts such as Hormuz (1507) and Goa (captured 1510) under Afonso de Albuquerque, to control key routes and tax trade.

The contrast matters: in the Indian Ocean, Europeans were one relatively weak newcomer trying to muscle into a powerful system. Portugal never controlled the whole of Indian Ocean trade, only parts of it, for a limited time.

vocab.def: Large empire centred on Tenochtitlan in central Mexico.
An agreement to work together, often against a common enemy.
Indigenous nation who allied with Cortés.
Taking control of a place or people by force.
Major Indian Ocean port on India's Malabar coast.
A strengthened military building used to control or defend territory.

misconceptions.wrong: A few hundred Spaniards defeated the Mexica with better weapons.
misconceptions.right: Tens of thousands of Indigenous allies and smallpox were usually more decisive.

misconceptions.wrong: Da Gama found an undeveloped world in India.
misconceptions.right: He entered a sophisticated trading system that was not impressed by his goods.
It controlled only parts of the trade, for a limited time.
Encounters in the Americas and the Indian Ocean were very different.

sources.title: Nahua pictorial accounts of the conquest (for example the Florentine Codex)
sources.origin: Made with Nahua (Indigenous Mexican) authors and artists under the Spanish friar Bernardino de Sahagún.
sources.purpose: To record Nahua history and culture, partly for Spanish missionaries.
sources.usefulness: Gives Indigenous perspectives on the conquest. Made decades later and shaped by Spanish supervision.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that Indigenous allies were vital to the fall of the Mexica.
evidence.model: The Tlaxcalans provided tens of thousands of warriors, while Cortés had only about 500–600 Spanish soldiers, so Indigenous allies vastly outnumbered the Spanish.

evidence.q: Explain one key difference between European experiences in the Americas and the Indian Ocean.
evidence.model: In the Americas, Spain helped bring down the Mexica Empire, but in the Indian Ocean Portugal was a relatively weak newcomer that could only control parts of trade through forts like Goa.

flashcards.a: Indigenous allies of Cortés: tens of thousands of warriors.
Mexica emperor killed by smallpox in 1520.
Spanish weapons alone did not win; allies and disease were more decisive.
A weak newcomer using force and forts; never controlled all trade.
Conquest of an empire in the Americas vs muscling into an existing system in the Indian Ocean.

questions.q: What can you learn from Source A about the fall of Tenochtitlan?

sources.label: Source A
sources.provenance: From the Florentine Codex, compiled in the 1570s by Nahua (Indigenous Mexican) authors and artists working with the Spanish friar Bernardino de Sahagún.
sources.text: One illustration shows Mexica people lying sick with smallpox, their bodies covered in sores, while others care for them. Other pages show Spanish soldiers fighting alongside thousands of Indigenous allies, and canoes and boats on the lake around Tenochtitlan during the siege.

questions.sources_note: Source A is described in our own words for revision practice. In the exam you will be given the source itself.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Spanish weapons were the main reason the Mexica Empire fell." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh technology against alliances, disease and politics, then judge.
steps: Explain how technology helped, with evidence.
Explain at least one other factor with stronger evidence.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

model.t: I largely disagree: Spanish weapons mattered, but Indigenous alliances were more important.
Cortés had only about 500–600 soldiers, but the Tlaxcalans provided tens of thousands of warriors.
This meant most of the fighting was done by Indigenous forces, and smallpox, which killed Cuitláhuac in 1520, further weakened the Mexica at a crucial moment.
Therefore weapons were a supporting factor, while alliances and disease were decisive.
